study.title: Revelation 1 The revelation of Jesus Christ, the vision of the Son of Man, and the sense of the seven churches
study.overview: Revelation 1 opens the book as a revelation given by God to Jesus Christ and transmitted through angel to John, with the purpose of making known to the churches what needs to be written and kept. The chapter unites prologue, greeting to the seven churches, testimony of John in Patmos and the majestic vision of Christ glorified in the midst of the candlesticks. The focus is not speculative curiosity, but fidelity, perseverance and worship before the one who lives forever, judges with justice and sustains his church.

outline.title: Origin of Revelation and Beatitude of Obedience
outline.explanation: Revelation comes from God through Jesus Christ and is transmitted to John to be read, heard and guarded. The text already anticipates that this word requires a practical answer and that time is near.

outline.title: Greeting to the churches and exaltation of Christ
outline.explanation: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace, speaks of the God who is, who was and who is to come, and describes Jesus as a faithful witness, the winner of death and universal king who will return visibly.

outline.title: John in Patmos and the vision of the glorified Christ
outline.explanation: John, in suffering because of the gospel, receives the vision in the Lord's day. Christ appears in the midst of the candlesticks, with attributes of holiness, authority, judgment and glory, which highlight his active presence among the churches.

outline.title: Fear, consolation and interpretation of the symbol
outline.explanation: John falls as dead, but Christ raises him up and reassures him. The Lord presents himself as the first and last, the dead who lives forever and what possesses the keys of death. Finally, he explains the mystery of the seven stars and the seven candlesticks as reference to the churches and their messengers.

study.context: The chapter presents the literary opening of the Apocalypse as a message sent to the seven churches of Asia. The notes indicate that Patmos was a place of exile and that John was there because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. The text also shows an angel-mediated form of prophetic communication marked by symbols, something characteristic of apocalyptic writing.
study.theology: This chapter teaches that the initiative of salvation and revelation belongs to God, but that the center of the message is Jesus Christ. He is the faithful witness, the crucified man who lives, the sovereign over kings and death, and the Lord who walks in the midst of the church. The vision highlights his divinity, his paschal victory, his authority over history and his pastoral presence among the people. The expression that the believers kings and priests have made points to an identity of service, access to God and participation in his kingdom. The language over the seven stars and seven candlesticks shows that Christ rules and knows deeply his churches, and that the Christian community is not abandoned to his own fate. The tension between present suffering and future hope also appears: John is in distress, but in the Kingdom and in the perseverance of Jesus; the church suffers, but awaits the coming of the one whoever will see.

scholarViews.insight: The expression "revelation" presents the book as apocalyptic literature, in which God communicates his message by symbols, numbers and images, having Jesus as origin and central subject.
Promised bliss encourages careful reading and study of prophecy, showing that the blessing is linked to hearing and keeping the words of the book, even when there are difficult parts.
The seven stars are explained as angels or messengers of the churches, and the seven candlesticks as the churches themselves, giving the symbol an interpretive meaning for community life.

questions: What changes in the way of reading Revelation when we see it first of all as a revelation of Jesus Christ, and not as a riddle for curious?
In what practical ways can the church today hear, guard and obey the prophecy of this chapter rather than just analysing it?
How does the image of Christ among the candlesticks correct our tendency to think that Jesus is far from the church struggles?
study.practice: Read Revelation 1 in prayer, asking for reverence and obedience before interpretation. Then observe three things: what the text states about Christ, what he asks of the churches and what comfort offers to those who suffer for remaining faithful. Take a concrete attitude this week to strengthen Christian perseverance: encourage another person, maintain fidelity in witness or persevere in prayer and Bible reading with attention to what has been understood.
study.uncertainty: There are important interpretative limits in the chapter. The notes do not definitively resolve who the seven stars are; they offer possibilities, with emphasis on the idea of church messengers. They also do not allow to affirm with absolute certainty, from this isolated chapter, the exact extent of expressions such as "coming soon" or "all eye will see" in chronological or historical terms. Reading about Christ's coming in judgment and the possible reference to the destruction of Jerusalem appears as an interpretation of some commentators, not as an undeniable conclusion of the text.
